analysis.one_liner: Defines domestic ocean shipping rates to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and Guam as unreasonable if more than 10% above international benchmarks.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in a House subcommittee since January 2025 with no vote and no further action, backed by only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a century-old shipping law, goods moved by sea between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other noncontiguous U.S. areas must travel on American-built, American-crewed ships. That requirement lets the carriers serving those routes charge far more than international shipping lines charge for similar distances. This bill would write a benchmark into law: a rate would count as reasonable — and therefore legal under existing rate rules — only if it stays within 10% of a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission. Shipper and consumer rates above that band could be challenged. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and nothing has happened since.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other noncontiguous U.S. areas, who pay shipping costs embedded in nearly everything they buy — food, cars, fuel, building materials. A rate benchmark tied to international prices would give them a legal standard to challenge inflated rates on the small number of carriers that serve these routes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends federal law so that a rate in noncontiguous domestic ocean trade is reasonable only if it is within 10% of a rate set by a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission [S2] [S3].

Current law requires these rates to be reasonable but provides no concrete benchmark, leaving shippers and residents to argue reasonableness in the abstract; the bill replaces that with a measurable standard [S2] [S3].

The trade it covers is exactly the one serving Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories, where a small set of carriers faces no international competition because of the domestic-shipping requirement.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flag ocean carriers serving the noncontiguous trades — companies whose business model depends on charging rates well above what international lines charge for comparable routes, because the law bars foreign competition. Their rates above the benchmark would become challengeable as unreasonable.

drawbacks.text: International rate indexes may not reflect the actual cost of running American-crewed, American-built ships, which face crew wages and build costs far above international norms; a rate within 10% of an international index could fall below cost on some routes, and carriers that exit would leave island communities with less frequent or less reliable service.
The bill states the benchmark but gives no detail on enforcement — who can challenge a rate and how — so its real-world effect depends on how the Federal Maritime Commission and courts implement it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of people in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories, shipping premiums are a real, recurring tax on daily life, and a concrete benchmark is a plausible check on it. The honest objection is real too: American-crewed ships are genuinely more expensive to operate, and if the benchmark squeezes carriers below viability, remote communities could end up with thinner service rather than cheaper service. The bill would work better paired with measures that lower the underlying cost of U.S.-flag operation; on its own it trades a clear consumer standard against some service risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in January 2025, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its maritime subcommittee, and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case of Hawaii and Delegate James Moylan of Guam introduced the bill on January 23, 2025 [S1] [S3].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and then to its Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation [S5].
The only action since is the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on February 4, 2025 [S5].
The bill has two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S.-flag carriers serving the noncontiguous trades are better off so far, because the benchmark that would make their premium rates challengeable has gone nowhere in committee. Residents of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and Guam keep paying shipping costs set without an international reference point.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small support is bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor from Hawaii and a Republican delegate from Guam, plus one more cosponsor from each party — and no member has recorded opposition, so no partisan line has formed.

industries.note: These carriers' rates on routes to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and Guam run well above international levels because federal law bars foreign competitors from the trade. The bill would make any rate more than 10% above an international index challengeable as unreasonable, directly threatening that premium. For consumers on those routes, the carrier's gain has been their cost.

If lower rates squeezed carriers' revenue, demand for expensive American-built ships could soften, though the bill does not touch the build requirement itself. The effect is indirect and secondary to the rate provision.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced with two cosponsors and referred only to a subcommittee rarely reach the floor. Unless the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee schedules a markup — which would likely require broader support and engagement from the affected carriers — this bill will probably sit until the Congress ends.
